title: XOR and the one-time pad
summary: The one cipher that is provably unbreakable, why it is almost never used, and how reusing its key destroys it.

steps.title: XOR: flip where the key has a 1
body: **XOR** (`^` in C#) compares two bits: the result is 1 when they differ.
```text
On bytes it works bit by bit: `0b1100 ^ 0b1010 = 0b0110`. Three properties make it the heart of most ciphers:
- `x ^ 0 = x` (zero changes nothing)
- `x ^ x = 0` (anything cancels itself)
- so `(p ^ k) ^ k = p`: XOR with the same key twice gets you back where you started.
Encryption is `p ^ k`, and decryption is the same operation again.

steps.explain: `1100 ^ 1010 = 0110`, which is 6. XOR with the key again restores 12.

steps.title: The one-time pad
body: The **one-time pad** XORs each message byte with a key byte: `c[i] = p[i] ^ k[i]`. Step through it encrypting and decrypting three letters.
It is **perfectly secret** (Shannon proved it in 1949) when all three rules hold:
1. the key is **truly random**,
2. the key is **as long as the message**,
3. the key is **never used again**.

Why perfect? For any ciphertext, every plaintext of that length is equally likely: one key turns `c` into `"YES"` and another turns it into `"NO!"`. The ciphertext alone tells an attacker nothing, however much computing power they have.

code: byte[] pad = { 23, 200, 77 };      // truly random, used once

steps.prompt: If the one-time pad is perfectly secure, why does the world use AES instead?
options: Every message needs fresh random key material as long as itself, delivered securely in advance
It was broken by quantum computers
steps.explain: If you could deliver a key as long as the message securely, you could have delivered the message that way. AES turns a short 32-byte key into a practically unlimited keystream, trading *perfect* secrecy for *computational* secrecy.

steps.title: XOR two byte arrays
steps.prompt: Write `byte[] Xor(byte[] a, byte[] b)` that returns a new array where `result[i] = a[i] ^ b[i]`. If the lengths differ, throw `ArgumentException`: a pad shorter than the message is not a one-time pad.
solution: if (a.Length != b.Length) throw new ArgumentException("Lengths must match.");
template: Dojo.Eq("Xor([12], [10])", new byte[] { 6 }, Xor(new byte[] { 12 }, new byte[] { 10 }));
Dojo.Eq("Xor twice with the same pad gives the message back", dojoP, Xor(Xor(dojoP, dojoK), dojoK));
Dojo.Eq("Xor with zeros changes nothing", dojoP, Xor(dojoP, new byte[6]));
Dojo.Eq("Xor with itself is all zeros", new byte[6], Xor(dojoK, dojoK));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("different lengths are rejected", () => Xor(new byte[3], new byte[2]));
Dojo.Check("the inputs are not modified", dojoP[0] == (byte)'A', "Xor changed its input array");
hints: Cast the result: `(byte)(a[i] ^ b[i])`, because `^` on bytes produces an `int`.

steps.title: Use the pad twice and it breaks
body: Encrypt two messages with the **same** pad:
```text
c1 = p1 ^ k
c2 = p2 ^ k
c1 ^ c2 = p1 ^ k ^ p2 ^ k = p1 ^ p2      (the key cancels out!)

An attacker holding both ciphertexts gets `p1 ^ p2` without knowing the key. If they know or guess **either** message (a file header, `"Dear "`, `{"user":`), they recover the other: `p2 = (c1 ^ c2) ^ p1`.

Soviet pads were reused in the 1940s, and the US *Venona* project read thousands of messages that way. In module 3 you will see the identical failure in modern AES-GCM when a **nonce** is reused, because GCM's encryption is "XOR with a keystream".

code: int c1 = p1[i] ^ k[i], c2 = p2[i] ^ k[i];
steps.explain: `c1 ^ c2` equals `p1 ^ p2`: `1^7=6`, `2^2=0`, `3^0=3`. The key never appears. Where the messages are equal the result is 0, which already leaks information.

steps.prompt: Two ciphertexts were made with the same one-time pad. What does an attacker need to recover the *second* message completely?
options: Only the first message (or a good guess at it)
steps.explain: `p2 = c1 ^ c2 ^ p1`. Known or guessable plaintext is everywhere, so reuse is fatal in practice.

steps.prompt: Arrange the attack on a reused pad, given ciphertexts `c1`, `c2` and a known first message `p1`.
lines: byte[] mixed = Xor(c1, c2);          // = p1 ^ p2, the key is gone
byte[] p2 = Xor(mixed, p1);          // remove the message we know
steps.explain: Once the key cancels out, the attacker only has to remove the known plaintext.

steps.title: Break a reused pad
prompt: A careless system encrypted two equal-length messages with the same pad. You intercepted both ciphertexts (`c1` and `c2`, given as hex in the starter), and you know the first message was `"MEET AT DAWN"`.
Write a program that prints the **second** message. You never learn the pad, and you do not need it.
starter: // Recover the second message and print it.
hints: Turn the result back into text with `Encoding.ASCII.GetString`.
